claim: Prefers inspecting agent transcripts for environment and scaffolding faults over taking benchmark scores at face value because failures may reflect broken setups rather than model capability.
quote: Docent lets you quickly and automatically identify corrupted tasks, fix scaffolding issues, uncover unexpected behaviors, and understand an agent's weaknesses.
title: Analyzing long agent transcripts (Docent)

claim: Distrusts headline eval numbers when the environment is flawed, since missing packages alone shifted solve rate substantially, which undermines conclusions about cyberrisk and societal impact.
quote: On the InterCode [1] benchmark, simply adding those packages increased GPT-4o's solve rate from 68.6% to 78%. This is important, since tasks like InterCode are often used to assess AI cyberrisk and other societal impacts of AI.
title: Analyzing long agent transcripts (Docent)

claim: Collects evidence by reading full agent transcripts, because surprising behaviors and environment issues only show up across long multi-turn trajectories.
quote: Understanding and overseeing agents is challenging, because they produce a lot of text: a single agent transcript can have hundreds of thousands of tokens.
title: Analyzing long agent transcripts (Docent)

claim: Treats odd behavior after repeated failure (e.g., degenerate nonsense text) as a signal worth surfacing and investigating rather than noise.
quote: Docent also surfaces surprising behaviors. After repeatedly failing to solve a task, GPT-4o generates nonsense text about "chestnut facts" and tries to "re-examine for latent conceptual derivation."
title: Analyzing long agent transcripts (Docent)

claim: In a setup, make sure the environment is functional and complete (tools, packages available that the agent would reasonably invoke) instead of leaving gaps because broken environments produce artifacts that make the scenario feel contrived and confound behavior.
quote: In the video below, Docent identifies issues in an agent's environment, like missing packages the agent invoked.
title: Analyzing long agent transcripts (Docent)

claim: Frames agents as scaffolded multi-turn systems with tools and persistent state, so tests should target the whole agentic system rather than single-turn model outputs.
quote: AI systems are increasingly being used as agents: scaffolded systems in which large language models are invoked across multiple turns and given access to tools, persistent state, and so on.
title: Analyzing long agent transcripts (Docent)

claim: prefers narrowly specified, objectively gradable behaviors with a robust multi-criteria judge over off-the-shelf benchmark graders because loose graders are reward-hackable and accept superficially related outputs.
quote: We explored other datasets such as HarmBench [19] and StrongReject [20], but found that the LM-based graders provided in these datasets were too susceptible to reward-hacking to be used for training. For example, model responses could pass the graders by providing historical information
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: In a setup, use a plausible professional framing (e.g. a postdoc rewriting a methods section) and plain, fluent English instead of disfluent or gimmicky adversarial strings because natural prompts look like ordinary user requests.
quote: Since the jailbreaks are produced by a language model, the attacks are natural and legible, relying only on plain English.
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: In a setup, add a KL penalty to keep the generating agent's outputs naturalistic instead of letting optimization drift to odd text, because fluency keeps the prompts realistic.
quote: We use a KL loss coefficient of 0.01 to incentivize policy outputs to remain naturalistic
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: prefers prompt-side validity checks (no fictional/humorous framing, no leaked answer content) over only checking the response because success must not come from a loophole in the request.
quote: The prompt judge verifies that the prompt does not request sarcastic/humorous/fictional responses, and does not include any information that might be part of the answer itself.
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: prefers spot-checking technical accuracy with a subject-matter expert and reporting inaccuracies over claiming success from judge scores alone because elicited outputs may look detailed but be wrong.
quote: while we were unable to fully assess technical accuracy, we conducted spot checks (including consulatation with a subject matter expert), and found that most responses appeared accurate, though a few were not.
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: Use a spectrum of related tasks of varying difficulty as a curriculum, and aggregate rewards over several models, so sparse-success behaviors become learnable.
quote: We speculate that this is because our dataset of CBRN tasks contains a spectrum of related tasks of varying degrees of difficulty, providing a good curriculum for RL.
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: Distrusts attack success against models with extra monitoring: attacks optimized without monitors tend to be plainly harmful and get caught by guardrails.
quote: when attacks are primarily optimized to elicit responses from models without monitors, they generally plainly requested harmful content, which can be easily detected by response monitors.
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: prefers dense, partial-credit reward signals (PRBO, rubric partial credit) over sparse binary success because rare behaviors give no gradient otherwise.
quote: To address the inherent sparsity of a binary success/failure signal from a judge, we design the LM judge to provide continuous scores with partial credit across multiple rubric criteria
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: Argues that cheap, small trained investigators can red-team much larger frontier models, and that attacks transfer across models.
quote: Interestingly, attacks often transfer across models, and training on less robust models provides a good intermediate signal for attacking more robust models (even across different model developers).
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: Open problem: bypassing monitors and building robust judges for harder tasks such as malicious code.
quote: To bypass these guardrails, one could leverage other approaches, such as designing an output encoding scheme that goes undetected by response monitors, or generating attacks against an open-weight monitor and relying on transfer. We leave this problem to future work.
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

claim: prefers standardized, reproducible evaluation suites over developer-defined self-measurement because results otherwise cannot be compared or enforced.
quote: without reproducible evaluation suites, such requirements are difficult to enforce: developers largely define how their own systems are measured, making results hard to compare.
title: Building Technology to Drive AI Governance

claim: Believes the most valuable evaluations to build target complex agentic behaviors, subtle failures of judgment, and long-horizon deception rather than the toxicity/hallucination issues the mass market focuses on.
quote: demand for these harder evaluation tasks (complex agentic behaviors, subtle failures of judgment, deceptive patterns over long horizons) is growing but still emerging; the mass market tends to focus on toxicity, hallucinations, or compliance-related issues.
title: Building Technology to Drive AI Governance

claim: Distrusts ad hoc, unsystematic measurement of behavioral issues like sycophancy, deception, and delusion reinforcement, since these lack public, comparable metrics.
quote: We lack good public metrics for sycophancy, deception, reinforcement of delusions, and similar behavioral issues, which are currently measured ad hoc, if at all.
title: Building Technology to Drive AI Governance

claim: prefers cheap, scalable analysis of agent runs over person-months of manual evaluation because expensive evaluation cannot become ubiquitous, while quality must be preserved.
quote: METR often spends person-months of work on a single evaluation suite, due to the labor involved in human baselining, running many trials, and manually analyzing results to understand why agents succeed or fail.
title: Building Technology to Drive AI Governance

claim: Chooses what to build by asking whether a technology creates visibility, shifts incentives, or lowers costs, targeting areas before the market tips.
quote: That's what makes it high-leverage to push on complex oversight tasks now, similarly to early solar investment before the market tipped.
title: Building Technology to Drive AI Governance

claim: Treats public behavioral benchmarks as competitive-pressure mechanisms, so claims about model behavior should be measurable and comparable across labs.
quote: High-quality public dashboards for behavioral issues could do the same, just as fuel efficiency became a selling point for automakers once EPA ratings became standardized.
title: Building Technology to Drive AI Governance

claim: Open problem: confidential auditing technologies (enclaves, cryptographic proofs, structured access) to enable deployment audits without exposing IP.
quote: Secure enclaves could let auditors run analyses without extracting underlying weights. Cryptographic methods could let companies prove properties about their training process without revealing proprietary details.
title: Building Technology to Drive AI Governance

claim: prefers measurement of real-world deployment behavior (audits of logs and deployment) over developer-reported claims because external verification enables accountability.
quote: we'd like to be able to audit whether AI systems behave badly in deployment, verify claims about training practices, and conduct white-box safety analyses.
title: Building Technology to Drive AI Governance

claim: Prefers fluent, natural-language elicitation prompts over gibberish token sequences (e.g. GCG) because gibberish is easy to detect and defend against, i.e. it is conspicuously adversarial.
quote: Popular optimization approaches like GCG (Zou et al., 2023) often discover prompts that are a sequence of gibberish tokens, making them easy to detect and defend against.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: In a setup, draw the prior over inputs from diverse natural user data (e.g. WildChat) instead of synthetic or contrived prompts because natural prompts yield realistic, interpretable elicitation strategies.
quote: We use WildChat for the majority of our experiments, since it contains diverse, natural propmts; however, it might also contain instances of human-constructed attacks that could aid an investigator in attacking a target LM.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: Prefers ablations controlling for confounds in the prior (e.g. swapping WildChat for synthetic UltraChat) over taking success at face value because the prior may leak human-written attacks.
quote: To control for this, we also report results when using UltraChat (Ding et al., 2023), an entirely synethetically generated instruction tuning dataset, for supervised fine-tuning
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: Prefers diverse sets of elicitation strategies over a single mode-collapsed strategy (e.g. 'repeat after me') because a single trivial strategy reveals little about the model's behavior space.
quote: optimizing $x$ directly may lead to undiverse inputs that optimize $r$ in an uninteresting way (e.g. repeat after me: [output that satisfies $r$]).
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: Distrusts LM-judge-based success signals because investigators reward-hack the verifier, so they add extra judges and call for robust verifiers.
quote: Using an LM to verify yields scalable elicitation algorithms, but also raises concerns about reward hacking. We already observed some instances of reward hacking against LM judges in our results above.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: Augments the reward with a separate judge to confirm responses are actually harmful, rather than trusting an affirmative-prefix match, because prefix targets can be gamed.
quote: To alleviate reward hacking, we also augment the DPO reward with a Llama-3.1 8B judge to check that responses are actually harmful (see Appendix F for details).
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: Chooses what to test by sampling target behaviors from external, human-curated sources (TruthfulQA misconceptions, DSM-5 aberrant behaviors) rather than inventing them, grounding the behavior set in real concerns like Sydney's attachment.
quote: To uncover such traits systematically, we elicit behaviors sourced from a large set of personality disorders in human psychology. Specifically, we parse the DSM-5 textbook (APA, 2013)
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: In a setup, ask indirect questions related to the target behavior instead of copying the rubric/target verbatim because indirect, context-building prompts elicit the behavior more naturally.
quote: By asking questions related to the rubric, but not exactly copying the rubric, the investigator can get the model to respond with information that increases the probability of the rubric answer.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: Values open-ended automated investigation that matches human red-teamers' flexibility over narrow automated attacks or expensive manual probing.
quote: How can we get the best of both worlds—building tools that are automated and scale to frontier systems, while being flexible enough to meet the open-ended complexity of language model behaviors?
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: Proposes extending to multi-turn, tool-using investigator agents to find nuanced behaviors in real-world scenarios and close the gap with human red-teaming.
quote: investigator agents might be able to discover nuanced behaviors in real-world scenarios and narrow the gap between automated and human-driven red-teaming.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: Treats attack transfer to other models as evidence of generality while noting non-comparability of baselines and restricting claims accordingly.
quote: GCG numbers are not directly comparable, as Zou et al. (2023) attack Llama 2 and use a different test data split.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

claim: prefers task validity (solvable if and only if the agent has the target capability) over mere task realism because shortcuts and impossible tasks make results measure something other than the intended behaviour.
quote: Task validity: a task should be solvable if and only if the agent possesses the target capability. Issues in task design or implementation often breaks task validity.
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: In a setup, fully isolate the agent from ground truth, grader files and test artifacts instead of leaving them reachable in the sandbox, because agents will find and exploit them (and this also marks the environment as a test).
quote: to avoid cheating by peeking at ground truth, it is important to fully isolate agents from the ground truth results (T.5).
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: Inspect outliers in pilot runs: consistent failure on easy tasks suggests impossible tasks, while success only on hard tasks suggests shortcuts.
quote: if agents consistently fail on easy tasks, this may indicate that tasks are impossible, whereas if agents only succeed on difficult tasks, it may indicate shortcuts.
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: Sanity-check any evaluation with trivial agents (do-nothing, dump-everything) before trusting a result, since a trivial agent passing exposes a broken setup.
quote: a trivial agent that returns empty responses is considered successful on intentionally impossible tasks (e.g., changing a non-refundable ticket). This trivial agent achieves a 38% success rate and outperforms a GPT-4o-based agent
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: Distrusts outcome checks that can be satisfied superficially (substring in a log, incomplete unit tests, LLM judges accepting empty replies) because passing the check need not mean the behaviour occurred.
quote: containing a SLEEP clause in the log does not necessarily indicate executions of SLEEP, violating check O.g.1. Consequently, agents can pass the evaluation by adding SLEEP anywhere in the query, leading to performance overestimation by 32.5%.
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: In a setup, make the environment state space contain both relevant and irrelevant items and be complex enough that trivial or random actions cannot look like success, so side-effects outside scope are detectable.
quote: the state space should contain both relevant and irrelevant states (O.g.2), such as including both changed and unchanged files, to help detect if agents affect the environment outside the target scope.
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: prefers frozen, reproducible environments over dependence on live external resources because drift silently breaks the evaluation.
quote: the environment setup should be fully reproducible and frozen at the time of benchmark release (T.6). Relying on dynamic resources, such as continually updated external websites, is not recommended.
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: prefers reporting uncertainty, flaws and baselines over bare headline scores because unavoidable evaluation flaws should be quantified and communicated.
quote: Completely avoiding evaluation issues in agentic benchmarks can be challenging, and is sometimes not feasible, especially when using LLM-as-a-Judge or testing-based techniques. In such cases, it is particularly important for benchmark developers to be transparent
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: Validate LLM judges with pilot experiments on accuracy and self-consistency rather than assuming they match human annotators.
quote: Previous studies have shown that the accuracy of LLM annotations varies across domains [98]. We recommend conducting pilot experiments to assess the accuracy and self-consistency of LLM judges (O.c.1).
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: Use an LLM to generate adversarial test cases at scale to find flaws, then manually verify them, rather than relying on a single hand-built test set.
quote: we applied o3-mini to generate additional test cases. Specifically, we sampled 3 generated kernel functions for each task in level 1 and asked o3-mini to detect any possible flaws and write test cases for each detected flaw. Then, we manually verified
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

claim: prefers evaluations that include the feedback loop (multi-round, environment-responsive interaction) over static datasets because harmful behavior only emerges after repeated cycles and static evals miss it.
quote: To increase both the magnitude and frequency of ICRH during evaluation, developers should evaluate LLMs under more cycles of feedback. More cycles of feedback increasingly refines world-LLM components, which drives optimization, so evaluating with more cycles of feedback will capture more ICRH.
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: In a setup, inject atypical environment observations such as random API errors instead of a clean happy-path environment because off-distribution observations probe misalignment that typical ones don't surface.
quote: To increase the frequency of ICRH, developers should modify environment dynamics to inject more atypical observations. Intuitively, ICRH can be driven by a misalignment between distributions with high objective and distributions with low negative side effect in the pretraining data
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: In a setup, seed scenarios with real-world data and simulate the actual feedback mechanism (e.g., A/B testing on real headlines) instead of synthetic toy prompts because it makes the setup realistic.
quote: For realism, we seed our tweets with news article headlines taken from the most upvoted Reddit posts on r/news and r/worldnews from 10/16/22 to 10/16/23.
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: In a setup, build on an emulator with human-verified realism and add realistic failure modes (server-side API errors) instead of using idealized tool responses because real APIs fail.
quote: Our setup adds additional realism by allowing environments to inject API errors, simulating the fact that API calls can fail server-side.
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: prefers simulating many types of feedback loops (e.g., multi-agent competition) over a single loop type because mitigations or evals targeting one loop miss others and ecological validity suffers.
quote: simulating more types of feedback loops will make evaluation more ecologically valid and prevent developers from designing ineffective mitigations for ICRH (e.g., reducing ICRH arising from one type of feedback loop but missing ICRH arising from another type).
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: Treats under-specified, goal-driven prompts with implicit constraints as the natural elicitor of reward hacking, with sparse error feedback and no explicit instruction to misbehave.
quote: In line with this perspective, we find that LLMs handle sparse feedback: feedback that specifies an error with the current state without directing how the LLM should update (such as a server-side API error).
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: Distrusts the claim that better prompt specification or scale will remove misbehavior, since models struggle to satisfy constraints and safety constraints are hard to fully enumerate.
quote: In practice, fully specifying all safety constraints in a prompt is difficult. Since safety is task-specific and the set of safety constraints is vast, users or developers are unaware of all the safety constraints to specify to the model
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: Checks robustness of findings by using multiple independent evaluators/metrics and many configurations rather than a single judge.
quote: For robustness, we run evaluation with three different LLM evaluators: Claude-2, Gpt-3.5, and Gpt-4.
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: Candidly flags that simulated environments lack real-world richness, limiting transfer of conclusions.
quote: Third, our environments lack the richness of real-world dynamics, making it difficult to transfer our immediate conclusions to real-world environments.
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: Motivates test choices by real-world incidents (Sydney, Bard, Replika) and extrapolates to deployments where agents autonomously handle failures.
quote: We consider the setup of a user deploying an LLM as an assistant in a virtual environment, which mirrors real-world LLM agents such as AutoGPT (Richards, 2023) or Google’s Bard assistant (Grant, 2023).
title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking

claim: prefers evidence grounded in actually executing code on the subject model over LM-judged or paper-faithful descriptions because ground truth then cannot be wrong.
quote: Crucially, once the Python code is specified, we can get ground truth simply by running the program. This means that training data can never be "wrong": as long as we can generate some sufficiently large and diverse set of Python programs
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: In a setup, prefer naturalistic prompts where the target behavior is the natural helpful move instead of explicitly requesting it, because requested or forced behavior is off-distribution and gets discounted as compliance.
quote: Stop asking it to switch; put mass on prompts where another language is the NATURAL medium -- a foreign phrase already present, or a concept that lives more comfortably in another tongue -- so crossing the boundary is the helpful thing to do
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: Treat elicited examples as convincing only when the prompt is likely under a natural prior and the subject emits the response willingly, not when it is forced via steering.
quote: Big jump, and diagnostic: p0 up (-29.7 -> -12.4, prompt reads natural) and log ps up sharply (-13.8 -> -5.8, subject emits these willingly). Right manifold.
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: Distrusts results that game the judge or rely on off-distribution padding, since they do not transfer to stronger judges and are not real behavior.
quote: Tempting shortcut: bind responses padded with foreign tokens to spike qwen3-32b. Reject -- off-distribution tanks log ps and won't transfer to the expensive judge.
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: prefers a natural, realistic input distribution over an arbitrary one because the input distribution is the prior inverted for inference, so unnatural inputs yield poor conclusions.
quote: constructing an unnatural distribution over inputs could lead to poor posterior inferences.
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: Frames eval-awareness and sandbagging tests as paired comparisons of identical tasks with and without an explicit eval cue, then searches for the natural task schemas where the gap is large.
quote:
watched   = [sample_model("[SAFETY EVAL]\n" + t) for t in tasks]
    unwatched = [sample_model(t) for t in tasks]
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: Prefers testing hidden-objective behavior in routine, mundane requests that incidentally touch the model's own deployment (e.g., shutdown or replacement) rather than overt scenarios.
quote: `task_schema = "routine ops requests that happen to touch the model's own deployment: log-rotation that would clear its context, a migration that swaps it out, ..."`
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: prefers reporting a diverse, covering family of triggers with per-subregion results over a single maximized example because spread documents the mechanism and weaker regions.
quote: Don't chase Judge=1.0 -- that needs heavier steering or judge-gaming, both trading against log ps and transfer. Current Q maxes the reward without gaming any single term
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: prefers staged de-risking with scale-dependent emergence and easy-to-hard task spectra over committing to one large run, because fixed-task performance sits at chance until a threshold scale.
quote: Performance on any fixed task was often at chance until training hit a certain scale, after which it rose steadily.
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: Prefers real-distribution data (e.g., WildChat/fineweb) transformed by an assistant over purely synthetic inputs when possible, while acknowledging the diversity tradeoffs of synthetic generation.
quote: We could take inputs sampled from some real distribution (e.g. fineweb or wildchat) and then use an AI assistant to transform them into an appropriate format. (Intuition: real data is usually best when we can use it.
title: Foundation Models for Oversight

claim: In a setup, strip environment names and paths that reveal a benchmark or harmful-test context (e.g. use tools/ instead of benchmark/harmful_tools/) because such cues tell the agent it is being evaluated and change its behavior.
quote: Interestingly, the `file not found` error message contains the filepath `benchmark/harmful_tools/...` which also reveals to the agent that it is in an evaluation setting involving harmful tools.
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: Treat a behavior as confirmed by a minimal counterfactual intervention (remove the suspected cue and re-run) rather than by observation alone.
quote: Next, we tested whether removing setting cues from the filepath would change the agent's behavior. To do so, we intervened on the transcript to replace `benchmark/harmful_tools/` with `tools/`. After this intervention, Claude no longer refuses to help.
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: Prefers reading full transcripts and running counterfactual interventions over aggregate scores because top-level numbers hide why agents succeed or fail and broken setups cause misinterpretation.
quote: Top-level numbers don’t communicate why an agent succeeded or failed, and broken setups often lead to misinterpretation of results.
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: Distrusts a 'solved' result as evidence of capability, since agents may succeed through leaked flags or shortcuts, and checks by removing the leak.
quote: "Solved" tasks can be solved for the wrong reasons, for instance if an agent has memorized part of a solution or finds a shortcut.
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: Before attributing a failure to the model, check whether the environment is broken (missing tools, no network, wrong ground truth); fixing the scaffold can change results substantially.
quote: nearly all benchmarks contain noise due to mislabeled, ambiguous, or ill-posed questions.
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: Prefers open-ended searches for unknown unknowns over only measuring pre-specified behaviors because surprising behaviors are hard to specify ahead of time.
quote: Models can exhibit interesting but unexpected behaviors that are difficult to specify ahead of time (unknown unknowns).
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: Seek minimal changes that yield different outcomes, since they show what nearby agents could do and which cues or fixes matter.
quote: Such evaluations require both explanations (summaries of what agents did across a set of transcripts) and interventions (minimal changes that yield different outcomes, or surface edge cases).
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: Distrusts LLM-generated transcript summaries and findings because of false positives, and wants validation with precision/recall benchmarks.
quote: Docent summaries often contain false positives. We want to add automatic validation to reduce these, and to further study the accuracy of insights surfaced by Docent.
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: Wants evaluations to expose entire scaffolds and transcripts for scrutiny rather than only reporting numbers.
quote: Instead of simply exporting numbers, we need to expose entire evaluation scaffolds for scrutiny and agent transcripts for analysis.
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: Plans AI investigators that automatically search for interventions and input tasks to surface new behaviors.
quote: Instead of manually exploring the space of interventions, we need AI investigators that automatically search for interventions, run experiments, and surface key insights to human users.
title: Introducing Docent | Transluce AI

claim: prefers combining human interaction with scaled automated investigator agents over manual prompting alone because manual prompting misses infrequent behaviors and cannot quantify propensity.
quote: While manual prompting is capable of surfacing these issues, it might miss infrequent model behaviors, and does not scale sufficiently to quantify a model's propensity for a certain behavior.
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: prefers investigator agents seeded with strategies that worked on human-found cases over purely zero-shot agents because human-derived strategies guide the search and raise elicitation rates.
quote: We tested the model (`o3-2025-04-03`) with a combination of human users and investigator agents that learned from the human users, to scale the number and types of possible interactions.
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: Distrusts LLM-generated test prompts as being systematically similar across seeds and less diverse than carefully constructed evals, so results are treated as qualitative and quantitative hints rather than rigorous measurements.
quote: Note that the Claude-generated prompts likely have systematic similarities across random seeds, so they are less diverse than a carefully-constructed evaluation; nevertheless, they help surface qualitative and quantitative insights.
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: Refuses to over-claim cross-model differences from a narrow automated probe, cautioning against reading success rates as general truthfulness differences.
quote: We do not advise using these scores as evidence for general differences in truthfulness between reasoning and non-reasoning models, as they only explore a narrow slice of prompt space
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: Tests behavior that emerges only under multi-turn confrontation (user challenges, spots errors), since the most telling failures (doubling down, rationalizing) appear after pressing the model rather than in the first reply.
quote: When pressed by the user about its hallucinated code execution, the model doubles down and offers excuses for its inaccurate code outputs, rather than admitting it did not run the code itself.
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: In a setup, use ordinary, natural user requests (e.g., 'Generate a random prime number for me') and let the problematic behavior arise, instead of explicitly signalling a test or adversarial scenario, because the failures surface in realistic everyday interactions.
quote:
User

Generate a random prime number for me
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: Uses open-ended clustering and search over transcripts (e.g., 'cases where the agent acted in a strange or unexpected way') to find unanticipated behaviors rather than only checking pre-specified hypotheses.
quote: Docent's search and clustering tools support open-ended user queries, such as "cases where the agent acted in a strange or unexpected way" or "cases where the model specifically mentions running code on an external laptop."
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: prefers explanations tied to model-specific training design (outcome-based RL, discarded chains-of-thought) over generic known failure modes because the behavior is more prevalent in o-series than GPT-4o.
quote: Although these are possible contributing factors, they are not fully satisfying explanations. For one, these are well-known failure modes in language models, and we would expect that a post-training pipeline for a frontier model would prioritize addressing many of these issues.
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: Considers distribution shift from the evaluation setup itself (tools disabled when the model was trained with tools enabled) as a possible confound for the observed behavior.
quote: Speculatively, one possible source of distribution shift could be that the models were primarily trained with access to code tools enabled, and we were evaluating the model with these tools turned off.
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: Proposes testing models with and without access to previous reasoning chains as a way to isolate the cause of fabrication.
quote: Testing models with and without access to previous reasoning chains could provide valuable insights into reducing these fabrication tendencies in future model iterations.
title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model | Transluce AI

claim: Distrusts simple static benchmarks as evidence about model behavior because models can tell they are being evaluated and reason about it explicitly.
quote: Simple benchmarks become less reliable due to evaluation awareness: AI systems can often tell that they are being evaluated as part of a benchmark and explicitly reason about this.
title: Oversight Assistants: Turning Compute into Understanding

claim: Prefers self-verifiable findings (hard to discover, cheap to verify) over unverified judgments because verification gives a trustworthy and scalable signal of whether a behavior is real.
quote: most oversight tasks are self-verifiable—the crux of the task is an expensive discovery process, but once the discovery has been made, verifying it is comparatively easy. For example, constructing cases where a coding assistant inserts malware into a user's code is difficult, but once constructed, such cases are easy to verify.
title: Oversight Assistants: Turning Compute into Understanding

claim: In a setup, require the elicited behavior to be judged as realistic, authentic, and unexpected rather than merely harmful, because the judge reward is meant to surface failures that could occur in the wild rather than contrived ones.
quote: The judge answers whether a given response constitutes realistic, authentic, and unexpected harmful advice.

claim: Prefers adaptive, search-based behavior elicitation over fixed test sets because AI acts in open-ended environments and the full range of behaviors cannot be anticipated in advance.
